Port Augusta, South Australia

Data of one day, AEMO, 5-minute intervals; replayed. Five real plants around the town follow what AEMO's 5-minute SCADA readings show: the solar fields glow with their output, the turbines turn with it, and the battery shows charging or discharging. Above the scene runs the real South Australian electricity price (region SA1) of each 5-minute dispatch interval. The day plays in a loop, 24 hours in three minutes.

Drag to turn, pinch or scroll to zoom, two fingers or right-drag to move, double-tap to go back. Drag the clock, the sun or the price line to move through the day. Tap a plant for its numbers.

What the picture means

Glow and rotor speed show each plant's output as a share of the maximum capacity in AEMO's registration list. That is a drawing, not the real rotor speed; the direction the rotors face is not in the data. Turbines (with hub height and rotor size from OpenStreetMap) are drawn about five times larger than life and the hills three times higher. Panel rows are drawn several times larger than life (8 m wide, 16 m apart) and the battery's containers about five times the size of a 40-foot shipping container (their number is a drawing, not a count). The buildings stand at life size on their outlines (simple ones squared to a rectangle) and are drawn half again as high. A few hundred are mapped in OpenStreetMap; most come from outlines a Microsoft model found in satellite and aerial pictures, so some are missing, merged or misplaced. Roof shapes, walls and windows are made up; so are the heights, except where that model's estimate is 3 m or more; the roofs take part of their colour from the satellite picture. The shadows of buildings and turbines are drawn from their shapes and the sun's position. Output is a SCADA reading at the start of each 5-minute interval, not metered energy. The ground and the gulf take their colour from a satellite picture taken one day earlier, on 15 Oct 2026 (about 11:30 local time, cloud-free); its light and shadows are those of that moment, mixed with the drawn light of the hour. Around the 62 by 44 km of the scene itself, the same picture and the same heights carry the land on to the horizon, coarser the farther out (to about 110 km from the centre), where it fades into a drawn haze. Close up, around the town and the plants, the ground's fine structure (streets, yards, tracks, creek lines) comes from an older, sharper black-and-white picture, taken between 2008 and 2010. It is older than the wind and solar farms: what was built since is missing in that fine structure, and what has gone since still shows. The colours, the water and the plants are those of 2026. Moving water is drawn where that picture shows open water (from its green and near-infrared light), so the shore is the one of that moment's tide; the ripples, the glitter and the soft glow around bright things are drawn. The hills' shadows are worked out from the drawn terrain and the sun's position, so they are longer than in life; the turbines' shadows are drawn too, and kept short when the sun is low. Close up, dark specks stand in for shrubs: a texture, not mapped plants. The sky is drawn from the sun's height; clouds and weather are not shown. The sun stands where it stood over Port Augusta at that time. The picture says nothing about what a plant earns, why its output was low, or how reliable it is: the data does not say.

Times are Port Augusta local time (ACDT, UTC+10:30). AEMO stamps its data in NEM time (UTC+10) and each value with the end of its 5-minute interval.

How it is made, piece by piece, with code and a reading list: Port Augusta, taken apart.

Sources

  • Plant output and price: AEMO, NEMweb public market data (Dispatch SCADA, unit MW; DispatchIS, SA1 regional reference price). Source: AEMO, used under its copyright permissions.
  • Capacities: AEMO, NEM Registration and Exemption List.
  • Exchange rate: ECB euro foreign exchange reference rate. Source: ECB statistics.
  • Terrain: Geoscience Australia, 1 second SRTM-derived Digital Elevation Model, CC BY 4.0; averaged to cells of about 210 by 250 m, the sea drawn from the OpenStreetMap coastline; slopes for the light at about 30 m; the wider land in cells of about 450 m.
  • Ground colour: satellite picture of 15 Oct 2026 (one day before the replayed day) from Geoscience Australia, DEA Surface Reflectance (Sentinel-2B MSI) (doi:10.26186/146551), © Commonwealth of Australia (Geoscience Australia), CC BY 4.0. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2026. Turned into true colour, colour-adjusted, sharpened and resampled to about 15 m; the wider land is the same pass at about 28 m (to about 55 km out) and about 112 m (beyond); the water outline comes from the green and near-infrared bands of the same pass, kept to low ground (heights above; the sea area from the OpenStreetMap coastline counts as low).
  • Fine ground detail: Geoscience Australia, Australian Geographic Reference Image (AGRI), 2.5 m, from ALOS PRISM pictures of 2006 to 2010 (here: 2008 to 2010; doi:10.4225/25/5524BA4A047FE), © Commonwealth of Australia (Geoscience Australia), CC BY 4.0. Reprojected; only what is finer than about 10 m is used, as light and dark over the 2026 colours.
  • Most house outlines and some heights: Microsoft, Global ML Building Footprints (release of 12 Nov 2026), under the CDLA Permissive 2.0; cut to the scene, left out where OpenStreetMap has the building.
  • Coast, roads, bridge, town, building outlines and plant sites: © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; lines and areas simplified, building outlines as mapped.

Only the five plants with their own AEMO data are drawn; other, smaller solar plants nearby are left out. Made with own WebGL code, no library. The terrain and map extract in data/scene.json, data/terrain.bin, data/relief.jpg (slopes from the same heights, sea from the OpenStreetMap coastline) and data/water.png (the water outline from the satellite pass, filtered with the heights and the OpenStreetMap sea area) is available under the ODbL (map) and CC BY 4.0 (heights, satellite data); data/ground.jpg, data/mid.jpg and data/outer.jpg (the satellite picture), data/midwater.png and data/outerwater.png (water outlines from it, filtered with the heights), data/outer.bin (heights of the wider land) and data/detail/ (the fine ground detail) under CC BY 4.0 with the credits above; data/buildings.bin (building outlines: OpenStreetMap's, and Microsoft's where OpenStreetMap has none, marked per building) is available under the ODbL; the Microsoft outlines come from data under the CDLA Permissive 2.0.

Best possible

The real battery's readings at these prices

A what-if, not the plant's accounts: energy is bought and sold at the regional price of each 5-minute interval, with no fees, loss factors or other income; 85 % of the energy bought comes back out (assumed); the battery starts empty and what is left at the end counts for nothing. The real battery's figure is its 5-minute readings at the same prices, each reading taken to hold for its interval: an estimate, not what the plant was paid. Batteries can also be paid for services that keep the grid steady; these data do not show them. “Best possible” is the best these three keys allow, worked out with every price known in advance, which nobody has.
